questions.title: What is cross-site scripting (XSS), and how does SAPUI5 help prevent it?
questions.description: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is an attack where an attacker manages to get their own JavaScript running in another user's browser, inside your app. It usually happens when data that someone else controls, like a product name, a comment, or a URL parameter, is inserted into the page as HTML instead of as plain text: if the "name" is , the browser runs the code. The script then runs with the victim's session and rights, so it can read data, send requests in their name, or change what they see. The defense is to never treat untrusted data as code or markup, and to encode it for the place where it is output. SAPUI5 helps a lot by default: standard controls escape their text properties when rendering (the RenderManager's text() method encodes every text), so binding a malicious name to a Text control just shows the characters. The risks come from features that output HTML on purpose: sap.ui.core.HTML (whose content is not sanitized unless sanitizeContent is set to true), sap.m.FormattedText (which allows only a safe list of tags and attributes), custom renderers that write raw HTML, and direct DOM manipulation like innerHTML or jQuery's html(). For those cases, use the encoding helpers in sap/base/security, like encodeXML for text in HTML, encodeURL for URL parts, and sanitizeHTML for HTML that must keep some markup. There are three kinds: stored XSS (saved in the database, like a product description, and shown to everyone who opens it), reflected XSS (comes in the URL and is echoed into the page), and DOM-based XSS (never reaches the server; client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the DOM). Besides HTML output, eval() and new Function() with untrusted strings are dangerous, and so are URLs: a sap.m.Link whose href comes from user data can carry a javascript: URL, which UI5 guards with the URL validator (URLListValidator). The general idea of UI5 security: the browser is not a trusted place, so the front end must avoid creating vulnerabilities, and the back end enforces the rules. UI5 protects you by default; the dangerous places are where you deliberately bypass the framework.
keyPoints: XSS: an attacker's script runs in another user's browser inside your app, with their session.
Cause: untrusted data inserted as HTML or code instead of as text.
UI5 controls escape text by default (RenderManager text()); binding to a Text is safe.
Risky: core:HTML (sanitizeContent false by default), raw HTML in renderers, innerHTML; use sap/base/security encoders.
Three kinds: stored, reflected, DOM-based. Also dangerous: eval/new Function and user-provided URLs (javascript:).

questions.title: What is clickjacking, and how do you protect a UI5 app against it?
questions.description: Clickjacking is an attack where a malicious website loads your app invisibly inside a frame (an iframe), places it on top of its own page, and tricks the user into clicking on it. The user thinks they are clicking a harmless button on the attacker's page ("Play video"), but the click actually lands on a button of your app, like Approve, Delete, or Transfer, which runs with the user's logged-in session. The protection is to control whether and by whom your app may be shown in a frame. On the server side, this is done with HTTP response headers: X-Frame-Options (DENY or SAMEORIGIN) or, more modern, the Content-Security-Policy directive frame-ancestors, which lists the sites allowed to frame the page. SAPUI5 adds its own client-side protection with the frameOptions configuration, set in the bootstrap (data-sap-ui-frame-options): deny never allows the app in a frame, trusted allows framing only by pages from the same origin (and, optionally, by origins approved by an allowlist service), and allow (the default) permits all framing. When framing is not allowed, UI5 blocks the app, so the user cannot interact with it. For apps that are not meant to be embedded, use deny or trusted, and configure the server headers as well. It is dangerous precisely because nothing is faked: the click, the session and the request are all real. With trusted, an allowlist of other origins can be given with data-sap-ui-frame-options-config. Technically, UI5 checks whether it runs inside a frame (window.top !== window.self) and whether that parent is allowed; if not, it blocks the app. Note that when the app must run inside an iframe-based launchpad (for example SAP Build Work Zone), deny would break it, so trusted with an allowlist is the right choice there. The front-end check alone can be bypassed, so a complete answer also names the server side: CSP frame-ancestors is the modern form and supersedes X-Frame-Options; on SAP BTP it is set in the app router, on ABAP in the ICF service.
keyPoints: Clickjacking: your app is loaded in an invisible frame and the user is tricked into clicking it.
Server protection: X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors headers.
UI5 frameOptions (data-sap-ui-frame-options): deny, trusted (same origin + allowlist), allow (default).
Use deny or trusted for apps that should not be embedded, together with the server headers.
trusted + data-sap-ui-frame-options-config allowlist for iframe-based launchpads; deny would break them.
CSP frame-ancestors supersedes X-Frame-Options; configure it in the app router (BTP) or ICF (ABAP).

examples.title: Frame options in the bootstrap and on the server
examples.code:
<script
  id="sap-ui-bootstrap"
  src="resources/sap-ui-core.js"
  data-sap-ui-frame-options="trusted"
  data-sap-ui-async="true">
</script>

<!-- HTTP response headers set by the server:
     X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
     Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' -->

questions.title: What is Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)?
questions.description: Browsers follow the same-origin policy: JavaScript on a page from one origin (the combination of protocol, host and port, like https://app.example.com) may not read responses from another origin, like https://api.other.com, so that a malicious website cannot read data from other sites using the user's cookies. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the standard way for a server to allow selected other origins anyway. When the app makes a cross-origin request, the browser adds an Origin header; the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the allowed origin), and for credentials, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. For requests that are not simple, such as those with custom headers like X-CSRF-Token or with methods like PUT and DELETE, the browser first sends a preflight request (OPTIONS) to ask whether the real request is allowed, and the server answers with the allowed methods and headers. If the answer does not allow it, the browser blocks the response. The CORS configuration is always done on the server, never in the UI code. Never allow all origins (*) for services with user data. In SAP landscapes, UI5 apps often avoid CORS entirely: during development, a proxy in the UI5 tooling (like fiori-tools-proxy) forwards service calls, and in production, the app and its services are served from the same origin, for example through the SAP Fiori launchpad, the ABAP front-end server, or the application router with destinations on SAP BTP. The key point for a UI5 developer: CORS is a server setting, not something you can fix in the front end; no UI5 configuration can grant a permission the server did not give. Server-to-server calls are not subject to the same-origin policy, which is why the development proxy works. The honest answer: in a properly set up SAP landscape you rarely configure CORS; you use a proxy in development and the app router or the ABAP server in production. Real CORS headers are only needed when a service must genuinely be called from another domain, and then the back-end team configures them.
keyPoints: Same-origin policy: scripts may not read responses from another origin (protocol + host + port).
CORS lets a server allow selected origins with Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and -Credentials).
Non-simple requests (custom headers, PUT/DELETE) trigger an OPTIONS preflight first.
Configured on the server only; SAP setups usually avoid CORS with proxies, the launchpad, or the app router.
Proxies avoid CORS because server-to-server calls ignore the same-origin policy; real CORS headers are rare in SAP setups.

examples.title: A CORS exchange
examples.code:
Preflight (browser, automatically):
  OPTIONS /odata/Products
  Origin: https://app.example.com
  Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
  Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, x-csrf-token

Server answer:
  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
  Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
  Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, x-csrf-token
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Then the real POST is sent, and its response can be read by the app.

examples.title: The development proxy in ui5.yaml
examples.code:
server:
  customMiddleware:
    - name: fiori-tools-proxy
      afterMiddleware: compression
      configuration:
        backend:
          - path: /sap
            url: https://my-backend.company.com
            client: "100"

questions.title: What do input validation and output encoding mean for secure programming?
questions.description: These are two complementary rules for handling data that comes from outside. Input validation means checking every input before using it: is it the expected type, length, format and range? For example, a quantity must be a positive integer, a date must be a real date, and an ID must match a pattern. In UI5, data types and constraints in bindings (like maxLength or minimum), custom data types, and value states help to validate input in the UI and give the user immediate feedback. But client-side validation is only for usability: an attacker can skip the UI and send requests directly, so the server must always validate everything again. Validation should use allowlists (what is allowed) rather than blocklists (what is forbidden), because attackers find ways around blocklists. Output encoding means converting data for the context where it is written, so it is always treated as data and never as code: HTML encoding for text inside HTML, URL encoding for URL parameters, JavaScript or CSS encoding for those contexts. UI5's controls encode their output automatically; when you build HTML, URLs, or scripts yourself, use the helpers in sap/base/security (encodeXML, encodeURL, encodeURLParameters, encodeJS, encodeCSS) and validate URLs with URLListValidator. Together, they prevent injection attacks like XSS. In UI5, "handleValidation": true in the manifest connects the data types to the message handling, so a failed constraint colors the field red and adds a message without controller code; for rules the standard types cannot express, write a custom data type or validate a whole block with a field group. The sentence a reviewer wants to hear: client-side validation is a convenience, not a security control; an attacker sends the HTTP request directly with curl. On the server, also validate authorization (may this user change this record?) and the business rules; in CAP, for example with @assert.range and @assert.format. For output encoding, the helpers map to contexts: encodeXML (HTML text or attribute), encodeJS (inside a JavaScript string), encodeURL (a URL part), encodeURLParameters (a query string), encodeCSS (a CSS value), plus sanitizeHTML. The old names URLWhitelist and jQuery.sap.validateUrl are replaced by URLListValidator. The mistake to avoid is encoding for the wrong context: encodeXML on a value that ends up inside a javascript: URL protects nothing.
keyPoints: Input validation: check type, length, format and range of every input, preferring allowlists.
UI5 types, constraints and custom types validate in the UI, but the server must validate again.
Output encoding: convert data for its output context (HTML, URL, JS, CSS) so it is never run as code.
UI5 controls encode automatically; for manual output use sap/base/security encoders and URLListValidator.
Client validation = convenience (handleValidation, types); server validation = security (CAP @assert.range / @assert.format).
Encode for the right context: encodeXML, encodeJS, encodeURL, encodeURLParameters, encodeCSS.

questions.title: What should you consider about user management / authentication and local storage in a UI5 app?
questions.description: Authentication (who is the user?) and authorization (what may they do?) are not done by the UI5 app itself, but by the platform it runs on: the SAP Fiori launchpad and the ABAP front-end server, or SAP BTP with the application router and the authorization service (XSUAA), using standards like SAML or OAuth and single sign-on. The app runs in an authenticated session, and every service call is checked by the back end. The most important rule: never rely on the UI for security. Hiding a button or disabling a field is only for usability; the back end must check every request, because anyone can call the service directly. Do not put credentials, API keys, or secrets into the app's code or configuration, since everything the browser loads can be read by anyone. Use the platform's session handling and timeouts, and log out cleanly. Local storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, and UI5's sap/ui/util/Storage wrapper) is a convenient key-value store in the browser, but it is not secure: it is not encrypted, it stays on the device (localStorage even after closing the browser), and any script running on the same origin, including an injected XSS script, can read it. So never store sensitive data there: no passwords, tokens, personal or business data. Use it only for harmless preferences, like a selected theme or a collapsed panel, and expect it to be empty or blocked. On SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry, the flow is: browser → app router → XSUAA / IAS → identity provider (SAML / OIDC); the app router is the single entry point, protects every route, redirects unauthenticated users and holds the session, and XSUAA issues a JWT with the user's scopes. xs-app.json declares which routes need authentication. Authorization is scopes and role collections, checked in the back end, in CAP with @requires and @restrict. On ABAP, the user logs on to the system, the app is served from the same system and inherits the session, and authorization is PFCG roles and authorization objects, checked in the Gateway service. The front end reads user information (for example the launchpad's UserInfo service) only for display and convenience. UI5's sap/ui/util/Storage wraps browser storage: Storage.Type.local persists, Storage.Type.session lasts for the tab, and the second argument is a key prefix that separates your keys from other apps on the same domain. Local storage is not sent to the server automatically (unlike a cookie), which makes some people think it is safer for tokens; the risk profile is different, not smaller. UI5 itself stores personalization and variants in the flexibility service on the server, not in local storage, because they must survive a device change and be governed.
keyPoints: Authentication and authorization are handled by the platform (launchpad, ABAP, BTP app router + XSUAA, SSO).
Never rely on the UI for security: hiding a button is not a permission check; the back end checks every request.
No credentials or secrets in the app's code or configuration.
localStorage is unencrypted, persistent, and readable by any script on the origin: only harmless preferences.
BTP: app router → XSUAA/IAS (JWT with scopes), xs-app.json routes, CAP @requires/@restrict. ABAP: PFCG roles in Gateway.
sap/ui/util/Storage(type, prefix); variants and personalization go to the flexibility service, not local storage.

questions.title: What is Checkmarx, and how is it used?
questions.description: Checkmarx is a static application security testing (SAST) tool: it analyzes the source code without running it, and looks for patterns that lead to security vulnerabilities. For JavaScript and UI5 apps, it finds issues like cross-site scripting (untrusted data reaching innerHTML, document.write, jQuery html() or an HTML control), use of eval or new Function with dynamic input, open redirects, unsafe URL handling, hard-coded passwords or keys, and the use of vulnerable functions. For each finding, it shows the data flow from the source (where untrusted data enters) to the sink (where it becomes dangerous). In SAP development, security scans with Checkmarx (or a comparable SAST tool) are part of the mandatory security process and of the CI pipelines, so code is scanned regularly and before release. Every finding must be assessed (audited): real problems are fixed, and false positives, where the data is not actually exploitable (for example because it is already encoded), are marked as "not exploitable" with a written justification, so they are not reported again. The goal is zero open, unassessed high-priority findings at release. Teams usually document rules for their own setup in internal wikis. Scans complement, but do not replace, secure coding and code reviews. Findings are classified High, Medium and Low, and a quality gate blocks the release if High findings remain open. SAST tools do not understand that UI5 escapes output by default, so framework calls are often flagged wrongly; a false positive must be justified and documented, never silently ignored, and renaming a variable to hide a pattern from the scanner is the worst possible response. Two honest points: SAST finds patterns, not logic flaws (it will never find "this endpoint forgot to check whether the user owns the record"), and it is one layer among several: dependency scanning for known CVEs in third-party libraries, and penetration testing of the running system. Advanced topics worth one sentence each: HTTPS/TLS everywhere with HSTS; cookie flags HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite; pinned and updated third-party libraries; and a Content Security Policy, the strongest single defense against XSS, which UI5 supports with CSP-compliant bootstrapping (no inline scripts, nonce support).
keyPoints: Checkmarx is a SAST tool: it scans source code for vulnerability patterns without running it.
For UI5/JS it finds XSS sinks, eval / new Function, open redirects, hard-coded secrets, and similar.
Findings show the data flow from source to sink; SAP pipelines run such scans regularly and before release.
Each finding is audited: fix real issues, mark false positives "not exploitable" with a justification.
High findings block the release; justify false positives, never hide patterns from the scanner.
SAST misses logic flaws; combine with dependency (CVE) scanning, pen tests, and CSP.
